## My Reasoning

I have farmed this land my whole life. My husband passed several years ago, my children are in the city, and I manage about 4 mu on my own — though I hire a neighbor's son to help with the heavy machine work. At my age I cannot do everything myself, but I know this soil.

In Quzhou we always plant winter wheat and then summer maize on the same ground — that rotation is what my family has done for generations. The wheat goes in around mid-October after the summer maize is off. The maize follows right after wheat harvest in June. That cycle feeds me and gives me something to sell. I would not change this. There is no reason to experiment.

For wheat, I will use the improved Jimai variety — the village supply shop sells it and my neighbor gets good yields from it. I have saved seeds before but the cooperative seeds do better. For maize I always buy hybrid seed — everyone does now, it yields more.

I irrigate wheat three times: once before winter sets in to protect the roots, once at jointing stage in spring, and once when the heads are filling. For maize I irrigate at planting if the soil is dry, and once more during grain fill. The groundwater here is deep and pumping costs money, so I do not waste it.

I apply compound fertilizer at base application and top-dress with urea in spring for wheat. I have always done roughly 18–20 kg of nitrogen per mu — that is what my father did and it works. For maize I apply a little more because the summer heat demands it. I do not do soil tests. I use what I know.

I also keep half a mu of garlic and cabbage near the house. That is for eating and for selling a little at the village market. I do that by hand, no machine needed.

I will spray wheat twice — once for powdery mildew in spring and once for aphids. Maize I spray once for corn borer. Nothing fancy.
